title: Lesson 4: Design Authority
description: The layer that keeps a growing practice coherent. What design authority is, why a system of many agents drifts without it, how to set standards that actually get followed, and how to run design reviews that are gates, not rubber stamps.

questions.question: What does design authority own that governance does not?
options: The state each agent can touch and the tools it may call.
The standard of quality and the power to reject work that fails it.
The schedule of which engagements run in which period.
The budget each engagement is allowed to spend.
questions.explanation: Governance bounds each agent's reach, while authority sets what counts as good and must be exercised continuously by a role with the standing to say no.

questions.question: What property turns a written standard into a real one?
options: It is written in a comprehensive document the team agrees to follow.
A senior person enforces it by reviewing every deliverable by hand.
The executor runs it without deciding to, because the standard is loadable into the work.
It is published once at the start and never revised.
questions.explanation: A standard that lives in a document people must choose to obey is only a suggestion; it becomes real when it is encoded into the mechanism the work runs on, so following the method produces the standard output.

questions.question: Why must a design reviewer be independent of the builder?
options: Because nobody reliably rejects their own work, so self-approval is a formality.
Because independent reviewers are cheaper to staff than builders.
Because independent reviewers work faster than the builder does.
Because the builder is usually unavailable when review is due.
questions.explanation: A review can only enforce the standard if it can say no, and the person closest to the work is biased toward it, so the approval must sit with a role that exists to be skeptical.
